utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, yesterday at the start of the hearing, you mentioned two incidents which, in your view, obstructed the proceedings with a witness detained in the UNDU. As a general observation, the Trial Chamber would advise the Defence to raise such issues directly with the Registry. By explaining what is done at the UNDU and why it's done, the Registry might have convinced you either that there was no room or that there was no reason for such an intervention. With regard to the first incident you mentioned, the one that happened last Friday, the Defence obviously assumed that after having provided documents to the detained witness in accordance with the UNDU regulations, the detained witness could bring these documents by himself to a proofing session. However, the regulations you referred to provide for the following under bullet point 3: "The detained witness is not permitted to enter the witness proofing session with any documents, since it is a non-privileged meeting." Our 3 September 2014 decision is, by no means, in conflict with that regulation. As to the second incident, a simple query to the Registry would have learned that the UN DU regulations, in fact, do not prohibit the counsel of a detained witness to share documents with his client during the proofing session and that the UNDU management has taken measures to avoid such an occurrence in the future. The witness can be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to show you a document and then gave up. Now I'm going to go back to it. This is the constitutional law of the Serbian region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It was prepared by your ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L1. It is tab 589. B/C/S page 2, line 5. English -- no, no, B/C/S -- sorry. B/C/S page 2 and English page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us whether this is the law that we started talking about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in Article 39 on page 5 of the original and page 13 in the English version. Could you please tell us why the constitutional law prescribes that it is valid temporarily until the Yugoslav crisis is solved and until a final constitutional status of the Serb District within Yugoslavia is established?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is rather self-explanatory, that our goal is clear. At the moment when we passed the constitutional law, we didn't know what the position of the Serb District was. Our main ambition was to remain part of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia or some other Yugoslavia that would possibly be created after the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Since it was premature at the moment when the constitutional law was passed to talk about the possible resolution of the crisis, we hedged ourselves, and that's why we said that the document would have a temporary validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now move on to other rules and regulations. Could you please tell us whether the Ministry of Justice drafted regulations within the sphere of justice?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Justice also draft the Law on Courts?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a complete set of the laws relative to courts, prosecutor's offices, misdemeanour courts. We drafted all that within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up L22 under tab 603.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What you see on the screen, is that the Law on Courts that was drafted by your ministry?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the law in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us just briefly which courts were established by that law.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We decide to have a three-tier competency of courts. First there was a basic court, then a superior court, and a district court which is also an appeals court. And there was a corresponding number of prosecutor's offices. As for why economic courts, we didn't have enough staff to set up an independent court of that nature which is why higher courts had departments for white-collar crime. When we passed this Law on Courts, we set up two basic courts, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic court in Vukovar with a temporary seat in Dalj and the basic court in Beli Manastir. There was just one superior court in Beli Manastir and there was a regional court in Vukovar with a temporary seat in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about the competencies of courts when it comes to criminal matter.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was fully prescribed by the law when it came to crimes for which the sentence was up to five years' imprisonment. Basic courts were competent for those. Appeals court for those are higher courts and higher courts were also in charge of the gravest crimes for which the sentence was more than five years' imprisonment. And then the second-instance court in those cases was a regional court which was the appeals court for the cases that were heard by the superior courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that appeals on judgements of higher courts were heard by?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regional court as the second-instance court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the preamble of this text we see that that law was passed on the 9th of October, 1991. Do you remember whether judges were elected at that time as well as public prosecutors that would be on those courts?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only some of the staff were elected because we didn't have enough personnel to fill up all the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what conditions had to be met by the judges and public prosecutors who were elected into those positions?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same conditions as before the war; i.e., they had to have a degree in law and they had to have passed a state bar exam. There were pressures at first to involve laypersons, citizens of repute, as members of those courts and prosecutor's offices were rejected by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When it came to the election of assessor judges, were those envisaged?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were envisaged. And I think that at first we elected assessor judges for the basic court, and then some ten or 15 days later, we also elected assessor judges for the higher court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the municipal Assembly of Beli Manastir passed certain regulations even before the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was established and those regulations concerned property, labour relations and similar things?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. The municipality of Beli Manastir was specific because they were not affected by war activities. They continued functioning even after the elections in Croatia. They passed their internal regulations, their bylaws. I have to tell you that I found a lot of unlawful parts in them. Later, they all had to be amended and adapted to the laws that we passed subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up L58 under tab 627.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see a decision to rescind the validity of the legal regulations of the Republic of Croatia. This was passed on the 1st of September. Do you know whether before this decision was passed, whether the authorities in Beli Manastir had consulted you about this decision?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they never consulted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P2157, at tab 639.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the screen, you can see a decision on the termination of employment and prohibition to return and stay in Baranja of all persons who were in enemy forces and people who helped them and their immediate family members. You can see at the end of the text that it was drafted and passed on the 1st September 1991. In the English translation, it is on page 2. This decision, was it passed after some consultation with the government or your ministry or you personally?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had been consulted, I would have never allowed the passing of this decision. It's a decision that I said already contains unlawful elements; in some ways, even discriminatory. I do not agree with such language, and I don't believe there should be prevention and sanction included against anyone. I mean, this is the kind of behaviour that we were already subjected to, and we had no right to subject others to such conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of influence did such decisions have. How did they relate to the regulations adopted by the Great National Assembly of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and later the government, and how did they relate to the Yugoslav regulations whose application was also envisaged?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our regulations, there were no such arrangements. After the passing of our own legislation, these decisions should have been harmonised partially or fully repealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information or reports that these decisions continued to be applied even after the government was established?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never had such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Justice have any jurisdiction over prisons in SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the most direct jurisdiction over the prisons we had established, because we were directly responsible for them. Those were two prisons: The one in Dalj and the one in Beli Manastir which was part of the investigation centre attached to the higher court of Beli Manastir, district court of Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who would be placed in such a prison?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only persons who were placed there by decision of the investigation centre or by a ruling of the judge of the basic or district court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in addition to those two prisons which were within the purview of the Ministry of Justice, there were some other prisons in Dalj or generally in SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any such prisons. The only thing I know is that, attached to every police station or every Secretariat for Internal Affairs, there was a remand prison for persons suspected of having committed crimes recently or much earlier. Such remand prisons existed. They were not under our purview. A person could be held in such a remand prison up to three days, according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was this prison controlled by the Ministry of Justice in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in that prison for the first and last time when it was opened. When you enter Dalj, the High Street of Dalj and then turn right, it was a building adapted from some previous purpose. It was next to a small church, and it was surrounded by private houses that were inhabited. We knew that it was inadequate and temporary because we had already started a renovation of the prison in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For how long was this prison in Dalj used?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was more than ten days because when it stopped operating, it was connected with an incident. Very quickly, within a very short time, all Serbs were placed in that prison, and the next day a large number of their friends and sympathizers came to release them, carrying weapons. The police stopped them from doing so and the prisoners remained there. But already the next morning, explosives were set up by the wall of the prison, probably with the intention of blowing up the wall and releasing the prisoners. The explosion damaged the wall of the prison and fortunately nobody was hurt. The explosion also damaged the church nearby. The windows and tiles on both buildings were shattered, and there was also damage to the private homes around. With the assistance of the prison guards, we continued to hold prisoners in that damaged building for a while but already the following morning they were moved to Beli Manastir. Then we abandoned that prison. It was no longer in our purview, and I don't know what happened to it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said "the church nearby was damaged," what kind of church was it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I can't say. It was a small place of worship. I don't know it was even operating, but I don't know if it was Orthodox or Catholic. I never asked. But it's true that it was damaged. The wall cracked. All the windows were shattered, the roof tiles fell off, but it was not destroyed. It didn't collapse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said a barrel of explosives was set there. How do you know that it was exactly there and not by the church?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police came and they made an on-site investigation and compiled a record; I didn't interfere with that. But you could see clearly where the primary explosion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the warden of that prison in Dalj, the one that was within the purview of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warden was one Mr. Zaric. I believe his name was Branislav. He later moved to Beli Manastir and continued to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was his training? What did he do before becoming the warden of the prison in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, as well as the others, was a prison guard before, and they worked in different prisons over Croatia in different ranks. I never inquired. He used to work in some prison in Lipovica or Gradiska, or maybe he worked even in the investigation centre. In any case, he was qualified for the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any representatives of international organisations visited the prisons in Dalj and Beli Manastir at the time of the existence of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this temporary prison in Dalj was opened and when the prison in Beli Manastir was opened, both Stevo Zaric and Mr. Kulic as the warden of the prison in Beli Manastir and myself insisted that the ICRC immediately register the existence of this prison. Records of prisoners were kept, and they were visited and inspected once a year. They did their job and we didn't interfere with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mean "they visited," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of the ICRC came once a week. They talked to the prisoners. They inquired after their health and general condition. And, to be quite honest, they often helped us get hold of some supplies, like toiletries, tinned food, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear of an incident that happened in Dalj on the 21st of September, 1991, wherein Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, extracted a number of people from one prison and these people were later found dead?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the prisons operated by people who were responsible to my ministry, nobody was taken. I never heard of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Goran Hadzic took out some detainees from that prison in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it ever discussed at a session of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it had been discussed, I would have heard it, but I'm telling you I never heard of any such thing. It was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know maybe that the police had reported to the judiciary of such an incident, the prosecutor's office, or judges?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they reported to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just objecting because the witness already said he's never heard of this incident, so how would he know whether it was reported or otherwise. So we're going into the realm of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you hear of any incident of 5 October 1991 wherein Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, took a group of Croatian prisoners from that prison or another prison - it doesn't matter - and their bodies were later found in the Jama river in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be very clear and precise: If I had heard of any of the incidents you just enumerated, regardless of the fact that it was outside of my work area, because I was a minister in the Ministry of Justice, I would have found a way to bring it to the notice of people who were responsible and to have this prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, generally speaking, what procedures were applied by prosecutor's offices and courts in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We applied federal legislation in terms of the criminal code and the Law on Criminal Procedure, and we applied the laws of Serbia in matters of criminal law. And that law, because of the objections I had to the law of Serbia, was the law that we changed the quickest and most radically. What was the basic feature of our changes? We abolished the death penalty, and we limited the term of imprisonment to 20 years. That was my principle and my understanding that I had always advocated even before as a lawyer and a prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly how did the legislation at the time treat serious crimes, such as murders, aggravated robbery, rapes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law that existed in Serbia that we initially enforced was broadly speaking the same as the law that existed in the Republic of Croatia before the amendments to the constitution and all that happened after the multi-party elections. All our people had been trained to work according to that Croatian legislation. The principles were the same. For every serious crime that involved a sentence of imprisonment over five years, an investigation was mandatory. For less serious crimes, you could file a criminal complaint directly. If there existed a well-grounded suspicion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Susa. Mr. Susa, the interpreters asked you to slow down because they have difficulty following you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I embarked on a subject that is my speciality so I speeded up. I will repeat more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you up to which point we have the translation so can you continue. You said for less serious crimes, you could file an indictment directly. So start again from there.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the prosecutor receives a criminal complaint from the police and finds that there is a suspicion that a crime was committed, he submits a request to conduct an investigation. That request is decided upon by an investigating judge. If the investigating judge agrees that there is a well-grounded suspicion that a crime has been committed, he issues a decision to carry out an investigation. As a rule, when serious crimes are involved, there is usually one of the possible four reasons to put the person in remand. The judge decides to put the suspect in remand -- excuse me. The prosecutor decides to put the suspect in remand, and the investigating judge has to approve it. Thirty days is the minimal term determined at the outset but it can also last very long, all the way up to the point when the reasons that led to placing the person in remand are no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, under the prevalent regulations what was the longest remand in custody before indictment -- the indictment was issued?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember the date when those laws were passed. That was on the 9th of October. That's when the judges were elected. Did they start working immediately, as soon as the laws were passed on the 9th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no technical capabilities in place for their work, and not all the judges and assessor judges were elected at that time. We did not have enough space. We did not have appropriate premises that could serve as courtrooms, let alone some other technical problems, such as the lack of typewriters, paper, and everything that is needed for the everyday operations of a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D1007, tab 164. 164.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the decisions. I'm sure that will you remember it because it bears your signature. This is about the beginning of operations of the basic court in Vukovar with a temporary seat in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The date mentioned here as the start of the operations of this prosecutor's office is the 4th of November, 1991. Is that the date when all the other judiciary bodies started operating?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. When the chief administrator of a body finds that all the conditions have been put in place for the start of operations, he informs me about that and I pass a decision of this nature. I couldn't pass a decision of this kind until I got a message from the people in the field that they had everything that was necessary to launch the operations of their institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1007 will be Exhibit D218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that there was this problem of the lack of equipment. Did judiciary bodies have vehicles at their disposal when they first started operating?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, they didn't have any vehicles at all. People often used their own private cars as company cars for as long as they had the money to buy fuel. Much later, we did receive some cars that were shared by two or three separate bodies. That was a prevalent body which marked pioneering stages of work. Most of my work boiled down to dealing with the marketing work, as it were. I toured Serbia to raise funds, collect equipment, and bring all that over to our region where we tried to create our own judiciary bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether vehicles were requested for the work of judiciary bodies?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very often such requests were made. I suppose that I got on people's nerves with my requests of that kind. I looked for them where there were some to be had. Particularly the military had them and they stored them at various places, and one such place was in Ilok. When I turned to the Ilok command to approve two or three cars for our use, they never even replied. They never even answered our letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D844. It is tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you can see here is one of the requests in respect of the procurement of vehicles. Is this one of the requests that was submitted by the judiciary bodies to the military, asking them to provide them with vehicles for official use?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that the heads of all the judiciary bodies signed this letter and stamped it to make it look very serious. However, it was all to no avail. Nothing came out of this letter, as well as of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us why were official vehicles needed? Why did the court -- courts need vehicles to deal with their criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that you have learned in this case that our territory was wide and long. Sometimes we had to travel 300 metres, on very scenic routes, from south to north, from east to west. How could you carry out an on-site inspection if you couldn't get there? Those on-site inspections were sometimes carried out by the military or the police alone, and when they reached us, there were some errors in them that were very hard to correct subsequently. If nobody else, at least an investigating judge had to be sent to the site of crime to carry out or be involved in an on-site investigation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D844 is Exhibit D219.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, could you please tell us whether the Yugoslav People's Army informed the judiciary bodies of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem about the crimes that they may have detected?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to be very clear and precise in that. The Yugoslav People's Army, in keeping with their authorities in the field, which constituted a zone of combat activities, was not supposed to inform us about anything. Despite that, we asked them to inform us so that we could make a contribution and so that we could get involved in dealing with some of the problems that appeared in the field. We noticed that very often their organs, which were the primary point of contact when it came to interviewing suspects or eye-witnesses or securing the site of crime, did not do their job properly. In most of the cases, we were never informed about any of the procedures that they may have carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, tab 674. It is P104.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the reports drafted by the security organ of the Yugoslav People's Army. This is concerning Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his conduct. We have several such reports, but I chose this one by way of example. This is about the murder of some imprisoned members of the ZNG and some other persons. Did you ever receive any reports about such crimes, especially involving Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, or reports that some proceedings had been instigated by the military judiciary bodies against him?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I personally never received any reports either from the people from the judiciary, which is particularly significant, or the military, which was not duty-bound to inform me about anything, especially about the crimes of this nature. It would have been only logical that this would have caused a reaction among the military judiciary bodies if this indeed had happened because this report was sent to military bodies. I don't know whether this really happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will continue talking about the judiciary bodies of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, on the one hand, and military bodies, on the other, and their jurisdictions. Before that, I wanted to raise another topic. When the military operations around Vukovar were over, did you go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us why you visited Vukovar once the military operations were over.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the eve of my departure for Vukovar, there was a regular session of the government in Erdut. And during that session, we received a report - the chairperson, Goran Hadzic, informed us about that - that on the following day, the operations for the liberation of Vukovar would be over the following day and that we should appear in Vukovar on that day. So it was, in a way, demanded from a majority of the ministers who were able to go to Vukovar to do so. We were to meet at Velepromet around noon. I received that information. I was already in the hallway, discussing certain things with some people, and as the secretary of the government was leaving the meeting hall, he conveyed the information to me. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Go on, go on.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following day, I got up. I didn't feel well. I was already coming done with a migraine that I suffer from --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Let's go back to the previous day and to the session of the government in Erdut. What should been the nature of your visit to Vukovar? What were you supposed to do there? What was the purpose of your visit? How did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood the whole situation was that it would have been a symbolic visit to Vukovar. We were supposed to see as many people as possible, and in most banal terms, that visit should have given us some political points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the nature of the meeting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never realised that until the moment I came to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether a government session should have taken place in Vukovar? Was there an agenda, or was that to be only an informal visit?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that it would be an informal visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I need to start objecting with regard to these contentious issues but this is a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness has the option to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the leading nature is that the -- Defence counsel is testifying for the witness. It is putting to the witness that this was an informal meeting without an agenda and, of course, the witness, being a Defence witness, is agreeing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the witness -- it is just clarification of the witness's answer in line 20. He stated that: "The way I understood the whole situation was that it would have been a symbolic visit to Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But then, Mr. Zivanovic, in line 24 -- in line 24, the question is: "What was the nature of the meeting in Vukovar?" And then the witness answers: "I never realised that until the moment I came to that meeting." But he didn't - and I would say you didn't allow him to - explain what the nature of the meeting was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll not -- I'll not insist on the answer to that question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you continue what you started to say about the 20th November when you had that migraine.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I don't need any suggestions to continue. And I thank both you and the Prosecutor. That morning, I already woke up with a slight headache. I was close to deciding not to go anywhere, but then my escort came to see me. He's actually my friend, Nikola Drpa, and he begged me to take that trip at all costs. He is a native of Vukovar, and I suppose he was keen to see in what condition his house was and his friends as well who remained there. He couldn't take the trip without me because if I was not going, the driver was staying with me in Belgrade. So I agreed to go. And now I can't remember whether we picked up Mr. Bogdan Vojnovic in Novi Sad and drove with him to Sid or we picked him up in Sid. At any rate, the four of us - Mr. Vojnovic, Mr. Drpa, the driver, Radoslav Zlatic, and myself - arrived in Vukovar around 10.30. The route was from Negoslavci, and the part of town where we arrived is called Petrova Gora. In that part of the city, the buildings were not destroyed, although you could see damage on the roofs and houses but all the buildings were standing. As you went towards the building of Velepromet, the crowds were thicker and thicker. Many passenger cars, buses, trucks and many pedestrians were crowding the streets. We parked there, and we continued on foot down the street which was supposed to take us to the house of Nikola Drpa. We left the building and the yard of Velepromet on the left. There I saw hundreds and hundreds of people moving about, and I noticed representatives of the ICRC, monitors of the European community in white. And when we had walked another 3- or 400 metres, the street starts going downhill and you get a panorama of the city, and then we beheld all the horror that Vukovar was at that time. I don't know if there was a single undamaged building. They were all unbelievably destroyed and only chimneys were pointing upwards. I don't know that city very well, but another couple of streets down, we started going downhill towards the right. Soldiers from the sanitization section were collecting bodies and probably preparing them for further transport. One of the soldiers asked where we were going, and we said -- in fact, Drpa explained where his house was, and the soldier said: But, people, there are still trip-wire mines there. You are walking on very dangerous ground. Still, we all continued and reached his house only to find that there was only one room of his house remaining. And there we found four or five half-drunken soldiers who were looting things from his house. Fortunately, it all ended well because, as far as I understood, they were even ready to shoot at us. So a bit confused and frightened, we returned to the Velepromet building. I believe that from arrival to Vukovar to Velepromet, we were there for one hour or 70 minutes, max.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on that 20th November, did you need any special permit to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already emphasised earlier, it was a precondition, it was a technical requirement to move from Sid to the combat zone. I know my driver went to get those permits because I didn't leave the car. He brought these permits, and we continued on our way. And on the check-point, we produced these permits and we were allowed to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was manning the check-point?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army. Only the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in Velepromet itself, did a meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to wait for that meeting to begin. In the yard of Velepromet, there was the little house where the police was, and in the yard, a huge number of people were standing. I saw Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, Goran Hadzic, Vitomir Devetak, but they were all standing in little clusters of people whom they obviously knew. I was standing with Vojislav [as interpreted] Vojnovic and people came up to him, people who knew him. They talked to him. I was just an observer. I had really nothing to talk about with these people. We spent a whole hour standing there. And it was becoming awkward. Of course, officers were milling around, going in and out of offices. It's a huge space. And then an officer showed up, a lieutenant-colonel, who invited us to go into the first room to the right of the entrance. He opened the door, and I believe Goran told us: Go in, please. So I went in too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many people were in that room?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you go into that room, which is rectangular, I would say, to the left of the door, and the door is to the extreme left of that room, right next to the door, there was a table against the wall and around it were chairs. And then tables were placed like in a classroom. I believe there were four rows of tables with two chairs by each table, so people were coming in and taking seats, and there were perhaps ten more people leaning against the wall. When we got in, I sat down, I believe it was the third bench from the door in the fourth row. Vojnovic sat down next to me and the others followed. At the head of the table, there was Dr. -- there was Mr. Hadzic. People were coming in and going out. If you ask how many people there were, I would say that at any time there were 30 people but that number varied all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just see if there are some points that are not clear on the record. First of all, you said you were standing in the yard of Velepromet with Vojislav Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was Bogdan Vojnovic. There is no such person as Vojislav Vojnovic. There is only Milos Vojnovic and Bogdan Vojnovic. Bogdan Vojnovic was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that Vojnovic sat down next to you, which Vojnovic you meant?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, there was no Milos Vojnovic in Velepromet, only Bogdan Vojnovic who was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean he wasn't standing next -- sitting next to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos? Milos was not there at the session in Velepromet. It was Bogdan who was in Velepromet with me, and he was sitting next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened later, once you sat down?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This lieutenant-colonel stood up, greeted us, and introduced himself. He said his name was Vojnovic. Now we have the third Vojnovic, and to avoid confusion, we have to be clear. And the confusion is still greater because I don't know to this day whether he is Vojnovic or Vojinovic, and it's not clear to me to this day. He started saying: As you see, the operations to liberate Vukovar are coming to an end. There are small pockets of resistance that will be overcome by the end of the day. And then came the first responses from Dr. Mladen Hadzic who interrupted the lieutenant-colonel, stood up and made a long introductory speech. And then he wound up more and more, getting ever rougher with this Vojnovic until he finally attacked him very fiercely about the way in which the army proceeded in Vukovar, resulting in a complete destruction of the city. To some point, I understood this emotional reaction of Dr. Mladen Hadzic, because probably a number of people in Vukovar realised that very day that their houses were destroyed. It was a difficult thing to take in, and they were finding it hard to deal with it. After this very harsh critique against the heavy-handedness of the army, some other people took the floor, including Slavko Dokmanovic, who was even rougher on this Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic and ended by saying it would have been better if nothing had been done. It would have been better if we had come to agreement with the Ustashas, if the city had remained standing, and then we would have later come to an arrangement how to divide it. Vitomir Devetak was next to speak, also condemning such a heavy use of equipment and weapons. And Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic defending -- defended himself with arguments that were to some point true. He said simply that they didn't have enough troops and that all the loss of life was too much so they opted for this way to proceed. All that is destroyed can be rebuilt, but people's lives cannot be recovered. I did not say anything in that discussion. There was no subject for me to react to. However, a subject was then broached by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic himself who said: As a result of the final operations, we now have a large number of prisoners, and those prisoners who will surrender today will be transported to three different destinations in Serbia. I believe he said - and I'm almost sure - that those were Sremska Mitrovica, Begejci, and Stajicevo. All this was fine but then he added: And then when we establish their exact number, when we establish their identity, we will enforce the rules and the procedure we have used so far, namely, an exchange all for all. Then I asked for the floor. I introduced myself, and I said: Lieutenant-Colonel, and what about crimes, the crimes that had continued for almost the whole past year? He answered: The war crimes are in the exclusive jurisdiction of the army. That was not in dispute, not then and not now. But I emphasised I didn't mean only war crimes. I meant crimes in their continuity, crimes about which, by that time, we had a pile of documentation. How were we going to know who committed these crimes unless we get hard evidence? Direct evidence that we can get by interrogating people who were not perpetrators maybe but have some knowledge. I said: You have to make it possible for professional interviews in pre-investigating and investigative procedures to take place so that we can get evidence on serious crimes and war crimes. We suggest that you give it a think and we will certainly come up a proposal that in all stages of this procedure, we be involved in Vukovar, both as investigators and as judges. He said: I am not the right person to talk about this. You can do that in the period that follows and approach somebody else. And he went on to say: I repeat, among these people, there are very few criminals. Most of them are people who were forcibly mobilised. I did not say any different. But, at that moment, Goran Hadzic asked for the floor and said: Lieutenant-Colonel, we have often discussed that there were many crimes committed. We don't know how many criminals there are. I will agree with you that their number is perhaps smaller than the numbers we have in mind now but we cannot know until these crimes are investigated who are the perpetrators. At this moment, unfortunately, all we know is that there are a large number of victims. He said also: You know that we, as the government, have taken a very clear stance and we do not identify the Croatian people with criminals, and we are perfectly aware that we will have to peacefully coexist in the future. By that time, Goran was standing. And then after saying this he, and perhaps Arkan with him, left the room. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic addressed us against and said: So we have finished with this subject. We are now introducing a military administration in Vukovar. I am the new commander of Vukovar and, please, if there are any problems that you think I can assist with, please approach me and we should perhaps have more frequent consultations in the future. So this discussion that took perhaps about an hour was over and we all started leaving. As I was passing through the gate, I saw Goran talking to somebody. He just asked me briefly: What did you agree about? I said: I don't really know. We will have to address a request, I don't know to whom, that we are allowed to be involved in the investigative proceedings. And after that, we got into the car and drove to Belgrade. All the rest I have already explained in my statement and in my evidence in the Slavko Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to remember which other government members attended that meeting that you have just described for us?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Dr. Mladen Hadzic. Perhaps I should start with Goran Hadzic. Vitomir Devetak, Bogdan Vojnovic, myself, Bogdan Vorkapic, Boro Bogunovic, Caslav Ocic, the government secretary, Jovan Pejakovic. I apologise. I can't remember anybody else. There may have been other people, but I can't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether a record was taken of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I suppose that some of the officers would have done that or perhaps Jovan Pejakovic. It was a government session so it would have been Jovan Pejakovic. Jovan Pejakovic was sitting somewhere in the back of the room and I never saw him before we actually started leaving the meeting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was a subsequent meeting at which the minutes from Velepromet were adopted?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no minutes taken at the session which was held at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, apart from Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, were there any other officers present at the meeting; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three or four men, perhaps even five. One of them was Major Sljivancanin. At the beginning of the meeting, he peeked through the door to see who was there and left. Apart from Vojnovic, who introduced himself to us, whom I didn't know, the others never introduced themselves to us and I didn't know them from before either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the meeting started, or in the course of the meeting, did anybody try to establish a quorum?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no quorum was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if anybody tried to explain why Ilija Kojic did not attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, nobody mentioned Ilija Kojic. Unfortunately, nobody did. At that time, Ilija Kojic was in Belgrade fighting for his life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the meeting, or in the course of the meeting, did anybody inform the attendees of the agenda?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no agenda. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic delivered a keynote address. He tackled the first topic. He was the one who had the floor all the time, and all of us intervened, some of us adequately, some of us less adequately. Some were shouting, some were not. It all depended on the emotional state of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody say that the agenda was the same as the previous meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the agenda was not the same. There was no agenda to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Did you stay throughout the meeting from the very beginning to the very end?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the clock, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. We'll take the first break, 30 minutes. We'll be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susa, I will continue with my questions about the meeting at Velepromet. Are you able to tell us if at this meeting, perhaps you requested an explanation as to where 1.500 prisoners were taken?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody spoke about the number of prisoners at that meeting. Knowing what the authority of the JNA was, I wouldn't even ask about any group of prisoners, knowing that they were completely under the jurisdiction of the Yugoslav People's Army. Had any of my colleagues spoken up and asked about it, I would have tried to explain to him what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting, did Goran Hadzic ask you if there was enough capacity to accommodate the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting in that room, Goran Hadzic didn't ask me anything. I've already told you what he asked me when we were in the Velepromet yard. But Goran Hadzic had to have known that our capacities were very slight in the Beli Manastir district prison where the maximum number we could accommodate was 120 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I should have rose faster, but these are very leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm a bit -- well, first of all, I'm a bit concerned by what Mr. Zivanovic just said on public record here, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You want to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody mention General Jefto Crnalic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if the people at the meeting were waiting for an officer of the JNA to appear with some news or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody told me that we were waiting for anyone, and I really couldn't conclude anything like that on the basis of anything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And before the end of the meeting, did an officer of the JNA appear who gave some sort of sign by nodding his head or something like that and then everybody left the room, and that's how the meeting concluded?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't leave the room after any officer appeared. I didn't notice anyone. I left the meeting when Mr. Vojnovic said that the meeting was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did any government member threaten the army at the meeting by saying that your units would be brought in from SBWS, units with arms, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no such threats, and we didn't have any armed forces to make threats with. There were raised voices and mutual quarrels, but nobody threatened anybody with any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to remember what you were wearing at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always wore an old military uniform that was comfortable and pleasant. I didn't have any other clothing, unfortunately. This was -- you know the sort of uniform that I'm talking about. It's an old work uniform of olive-drab colour. I'm not really good as describing it, but I think you know the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember what the other people were wearing? I'm not talking about the JNA officers but the others who were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Vojnovic, who was closest to me, was carrying civilian clothing. He was wearing some sort of thick jacket. All the others were wearing military uniforms, newer ones, older ones. There were different kinds of uniform. Most of them were wearing brown uniforms and some of them were wearing camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if anybody wore blue police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice anybody wearing that kind of uniform, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did anyone say that the prisoners had to be physically eliminated?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember if Dr. Vojislav Vukcevic was present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Vojislav Vukcevic was my professor from Osijek. He taught civil material law. I knew him very well. He wasn't at the meeting. Had he been there, I would have definitely been sitting next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if Vojin Dabic was at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojin Dabic was not at the meeting. The first time I saw him and met him was during the negotiations with the Croatian side, in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Ljuban Devetak, was he at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Ljuban Devetak in Lovas during a very large meeting. Vitomir Devetak was the one who was at the meeting. Ljuban was not at the meeting in Velepromet; it was Vitomir who attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Ljuban Devetak was doing in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to Lovas, I found out that he was the director of the agricultural combine there -- agricultural co-operative there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the crimes that were committed in Vukovar around the time when the military operations were being brought to an end. Did the government have a position with regard to those crimes of which they were informed as having been committed before and during the military operations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the government's position. It was everybody's position and everywhere. The position is that perpetrators of crimes should be taken to task, and that was also the government's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you the transcript of a video-clip, a part of a video footage, actually. You will see Goran Hadzic's words. I'm not going to play the video itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P58, tab 709. I'm interested in the second page in the original and in the English translation. You will see -- in the original it will be the first paragraph where Goran Hadzic is saying something and in the English translation it will be in the last paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He says as follows: "As I said, I'm not concerned with the military issue. I'm positive about the final solution. However, I'm concerned because I received information from some of our services. They tell me that the situation in Zagreb, and we know what happened in Vukovar, that large-scale crime was committed against the civilian population. We will investigate that and we will bring perpetrators before an international -- a national court, or a people's court. I am certain that they will be punished according to what they did." Could you please tell us whether these words uttered by Goran Hadzic with regard to processing those crimes reflect the position of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, after the meeting at Velepromet, did you undertake any measures and make sure that the judiciary of SBWS got involved in the investigations of the imprisoned members of the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milos Vojnovic was in charge of the technical part of the job. On one occasion, he informed me who his collocutor was on the other side as opposed to address him for a permit [as interpreted]. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic pointed that to me. Milos Vojnovic and I drafted a letter to the commander of the 1st Military District. We received an answer. Milos set up a team of investigators, and they embarked on the job on the task at hand in the penal correctional facility in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P3262. It is tab 301.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at the screen. There is a letter on it. Could you please tell us whether this is the letter that you sent to the command of the 1st Army District?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether your request was met.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you go to Sremska Mitrovica? Did you go and visit this correctional and penal facility in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions, the first time and the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe your first visit to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, I went together with the investigating judges. We reported to the superior officer there. They entered the facility, not immediately. We were informed that the officer in charge was waiting for us in the hotel which was part of the correctional facility. We went there. Several officers of the JNA were already there. The judges were allowed to go to their rooms, and then they returned to the lobby. We were all sitting there, talking, having cups of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you enter the prison? Did you see the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And according to the information that I received from the judges, the judges were able to do that a few hours later. On that occasion, I myself did not enter the correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the judges who were with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jovan Ajdukovic, Grujo Amidzic, Slobodan Kovacevic, and three or four colleagues whom I didn't know that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you talk to on that occasion; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to all the officers. In other words, we all participated in the talks. And the person whom I perceived as their boss and who introduced himself as Branko Ruzic is who talked to us as well. But then, at the end of that conversation, he told us that he wasn't Branko Ruzic but Bogdan Vujic. I found that very strange. He told me: That's common practice amongst us. We don't always give people our real name. I found that a bit funny and I asked him: So are you Bogdan? And he said: Yes, I am Bogdan Vujic. I talked to him, he was seated next to me. We were drinking coffee. We did not discuss the topic which brought the people to the correctional facility in the first place. We discussed general topics more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about the scope of authority that these officers had vis-à-vis the prisoners? Did they have the decision-making power, were they able to decide what measures to undertake against them?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them, I believe that it was Mr. Bogdan Vujic who said that they were just an operative group involved in pre-investigation procedures which is only normal. And he said that we -- they don't make any decisions regarding the prisoners, that it will be somebody else elsewhere who will make those decisions. I suppose that he had in mind the command in Belgrade and I found that normal and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any other officer? Do you remember the names of any other officers?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember their names. They probably introduced themselves to me, but I don't remember their names. The only name I do remember is Mr. Vujic's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how come you remember his name and not any others?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Bogdan Vujic and I continued meeting directly and indirectly. On that day when I was leaving the parking lot in front of the correctional and penal facility in Sremska Mitrovica, my driver and my escort were standing right next to me. Mr. Vujic appeared from the correctional facility. He approached me in a haste. He was carrying a transparent plastic bag in his hand. When he was some 2 or 3 metres away from us, I realised that that was a big bag, that it contained some 15 kilos of money, German marks. He extended his hand. He gave me that bag and he told me: This is yours. Take that to the people of Vukovar. I said: That's all fantastic, but, Mr. Vujic, I have time, why don't we make a record of this hand-over? Why don't we count the money? Why don't you sign a hand-over note? Why don't I sign a receipt for that money? And he says: Listen, are you taking the money or not? I said: Yes, I will take it but in the manner that I've just described to you. He turned around and he said: It's very clear that you don't need this money, and he left. I complained about what he did even to some military personnel whom I know -- whom I knew and with whom I was on good terms. I suppose that the word reached him eventually. On one occasion, he sent me a very ugly and very strange message through my driver, and the message was that I would have a lot of problems. I don't know why. He didn't tell me why. He wasn't specific with this regard. My driver conveyed the message to me, and his advice was: I don't know what this is about, but you should watch what you do. You should be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last paragraph in this letter of yours, which we see on the screen. It says here that volunteers and members of the TO have committed a number of offences against property and that military police organs confiscated items from them, and so on and so forth. What's this about? What does this part of your letter refer to?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not read all of it, did you? I didn't say that it was done only by members of volunteer units and some members of TO units. I said that, unfortunately, some members of the JNA were involved in some dealings as well -- in the same dealings as well. That area was very affluent before the war, as you probably know, and even after the war destructions, a lot of property was left over. Cars, combines, valuable assets used in agricultural, household appliances, and things like that. And it was a common practice that some higher ranking officers also subscribed to. All that was war booty, and those assets were continuously driven away from the area. In one part of my letter, I point to that as well. The value of that property would have been huge for everybody, and especially for us, under such conditions, and losing such valuable property made us even poorer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you refuse to take the money that was offered to you by Mr. Vujic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a cautious man. I behave in accordance with the law. I really couldn't assume how much money was in that bag. I knew of similar instances where things were not recorded properly, and it was all about hearsay as to what was received, what was given, and it was simply unacceptable for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion when you were offered money and when you turned the offer down, was there anybody else there besides you and Vujic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned them, Nikola Drpa and Radoslav Zlatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that Vujic sent you messages through your driver. What messages were those?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between my first and second visits to the correctional facility, my driver went there on his own several times. He carried documents and personal effects to the judges who were there. On the second or third occasion when he went on his own, Bogdan Vujic told him that he should convey a message to me, and that was that as a result of my conduct, I was -- I would suffer grave consequences. And I took that to be a very serious threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of conduct of yours provoked him to react in such a way?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that -- no conduct of mine should have provoked such a reaction. You should ask him what irritated him in my behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that first trip -- I mean, you said you were in Mitrovica twice. Can you describe the second trip, how did it come about and why?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time I went to Sremska Mitrovica, it had been planned after I received disturbing reports from the judges there. My contact person was Jovan Ajdukovic, and once he called me on the phone and said he was calling me from a telephone outside the KPD and outside the hotel because there were serious problems in their communication with JNA officers, or, that is to say, their team that was doing the triage of prisoners. He explained that they were not allowed to have contact with prisoners, not even in the presence of the JNA on which they hadn't insisted in the first place, but they were finally allowed to have that contact. However, they were not allowed to question prisoners as they wanted to, and instead the army made them put questions that were pointless. He was especially disturbed by the fact that from the list that would be delivered to them when they wanted to contact somebody, they would regularly be informed that these people were no longer in the KPD, and this report was confirmed to me by some civilian officers in the KPD guards team. It was very serious, in his view, and he addressed Vujic and asked how is it possible that people were disappearing from this list? What rulings were made in their respect? What procedure is applied? Vujic told him that everything he was saying, he should put on paper. Ajdukovic did that, took it to Vujic's office. Vujic read it and threw it in the wastebasket. Ajdukovic said he was no longer willing to continue working like that and that I should receive his report and organise their return to Vukovar. He said he had spoken to all the colleagues. They all shared his opinion. So I answered: All right, Jovan. I will come tomorrow and organise that you leave this project, return home, and take up some work which is more adequate. I informed the secretary of the government, Jovan Pejakovic, that I would be going to Vukovar -- to Mitrovica the next day, as I normally informed everyone that I would not be in Erdut on a particular day. I don't know if the others did the same, but I always did it. And then I was told by Pejakovic: Goran is also going there tomorrow. He didn't say when, but I organised my time and my schedule so as to be in the KPD at the same time as Goran. Goran himself didn't tell me anything. Anyway, the next day, we met outside the building of the KPD. Japundzic and Mudrinic were together with Goran as well as the minister of the interior, Boro Bogunovic. I told Goran why I had come, but I didn't understand what his business there was. He said: These people invited me for some sort of discussion. That was all. So I didn't really understand why he had come there. We went in together, into the hotel. At the hotel, we were met by officers, including Mr. Bogdan Vujic with whom I had no further communication. The talk was very general, about the political situation, about the situation on the ground, about Vukovar, about various problems. And then at one point, one of these officers - but not Bogdan Vujic - suggested to Goran that he should go into the KPD compound and meet with prisoners, and he said -- that person said: Don't be afraid. It's completely safe. As I saw it, it was some sort of provocation, because if Goran refused, he would look like a coward, who was afraid. So Goran said: All right, I'll go. And I decided to go with him. Again, Drpa and Zlatic and Goran's escorts and Boro Bogunovic went with us. There were a number of officers as well -- as well as prisoner guards. We went into the KPD and that was the first time I ever went into KPD Mitrovica in my life. We descended into those rooms. It was a very old prison, built at the time of Maria Therese [phoen], with huge dorms with 40 or 50 beds each, and one of the large cells was opened for us. When we came, everybody inside stood up by their beds, and we went in 2 or 3 metres in the room. Goran greeted the people, and addressed the first officer standing next to him, saying: Do you give these people baths at all? He really wasn't used to this. It's true that it was winter, but in a place housing so many people, it's difficult to maintain hygiene and there was a very stale, unpleasant smell in the room. I don't know what this officer answered. Many of the people inside recognised Goran and shouted to him: Goran. Asked him questions. He told them: I know you are not really comfortable here, but it won't last forever. It will come to an end. I'm sure that most of you are innocent and you will be going to your homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this happened yesterday and I didn't object. But these narratives which go on for 15, 20 minutes, it's not conducive to the form of adjudication that we have in this Tribunal and we object to this way of eliciting evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not understand the objection. The witness spoke -- speaks about acts and conduct of the accused. I don't know what is for objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I can explain it, Your Honours, if you wish, to Mr. Zivanovic. But in an adversarial proceeding such as this one, evidence is elicited through question and answer, and we don't have any questions here. We just have a very, very long answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please try to focus on questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. My question, in fact, was limited to the purpose of your visit to the KP Dom. You already explained what that visit was like. Did Goran Hadzic speak to the prisoners during that visit?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did he question anybody?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were 60 people there, and they were all talking to him and he to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long were you inside the prison where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you together all the time, you and Goran Hadzic, or did you go separate ways at some point while you were there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all together in a group in a space of about 7 or 8 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the prisoners say anything to Goran Hadzic? Did they address him?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they put to him various questions. One of them was important to me. People were complaining they were returning out of cigarettes, they didn't have enough, and I understood that perfectly well because it would be difficult for me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, were JNA officers there? Did they withdraw at some point and leave you alone?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were there, did any of you, Goran Hadzic, yourself, or any of the officers or military personnel use any force against the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had received the report about some people who used to be on a list and then disappeared. Did you find anything out about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out very easily ourselves. Some of these people were sent away to be exchanged, which was perfectly fine, and some others paid their way to Croatia through their relatives and friends, and that was not all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P3200. It is tab 587.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a letter concerning this visit that was sent by the warden of the prison to the Security Administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. Is this the date when you visited Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correctly described in this letter that you came in order to establish co-operation with the operative team that was questioning the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We thought we had already established that co-operation, and we already had the approval of the higher command. That's why we came. In fact, I came in order to stop that co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are also mentioned in this letter. It is said that you had visited SV, in fact, the sports hall Pinki, with some delegation. Did you go to this sports centre, Pinki, and did you meet some JNA officers there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
