utterances.text: I suppose it's the sports centre Pinki which is not in Belgrade. The only sports centre called Pinki is the one I know in Belgrade. I don't know about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps go to the sports centre Pinki in Belgrade for the purpose described in this letter?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course, I went there for sports events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says in this letter that before coming here, you had tried to get into the prison and you were not allowed to. Did you, indeed, go to Sremska Mitrovica before and were refused access to the prison?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We waited for a permission of the competent authority, and once we received that permission, we were given access to the prison without any further problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps come earlier without a permit and denied access?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would we have done that? We knew we had to have a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that discussion, did you mention that they were letting Ustashas go?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular discussion, we did not talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you went to the prison, did you also go to the Red Cross in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there would be an exchange of about 900 persons that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the extent and the pace of the exchanges conducted by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in conversations at the time, did you or anyone else mention Dr. Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Dr. Vesna Bosanac. And I don't think that she was on the list that our investigative organs were taking to the KPD Mitrovica. They did have a list of some 20 to 30 persons. I don't know in which context I would have mentioned her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit more precise about those on the list, the 30 -- the 20 or 30 persons.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were persons suspected of committing a number of serious crimes, including elements of war crimes in Vukovar and its environs in 1990 and 1991. This is something that the victims and witnesses talked about, and this was raw material that needed to be corroborated in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you mention Saljic in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I did not. I do know Judge Saljic. He himself had a lot of remarks as a military investigating judge about the proceedings in Mitrovica. He wasn't even allowed to do his job. But I did not say anything about Judge Saljic. They perhaps just concluded that we were on the same side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me when you found out that Judge Saljic had similar problems. Was it at the time when you went to Mitrovica or some other time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at a different time. I met him in Vukovar in Milos Vojnovic's office, and he told me that. We didn't really get on so well, but that he also as a military investigating judge had to abandon the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in Mitrovica at that time, did you or anyone else from your group blame General Aleksandar Vasiljevic for anything?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know General Aleksandar Vasiljevic. I don't know anything about his work, and I don't blame him for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an ultimatum by you or the government that nobody could be released from the Sremska Mitrovica KPD without your permission, the permission of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that would mean that if they failed to respect that, that we would attack Serbia, because this was located in Serbia. No, we definitely did not issue an ultimatum to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that you toured three prison rooms at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the one that we visited. There was no other second or third room, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask for lists of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, but the investigating judge -- judges that were working in the KPD did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, were those lists requested during this visit or was this done at some other time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I never asked for the list. But I do know that the investigating judges, when they entered and started their work in the KPD, did ask for the lists in order to be able to see who was on them, who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did they get these lists?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with not all the information. There was never a definitive list as to how many people there were and which ones were no longer on the list and why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you say anything to the effect that the prisoners there were too comfortable, that the accommodation was too good, and that it shouldn't be like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accommodation was very poor. There could be no worse conditions, unless they kept outside without any roof over their heads. No, of course I did not make any comments about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did anybody from your group say anything to that effect? I'm thinking of you who were all there together on the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you object because the prisoners were smoking?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would never object to anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when I say "you," I don't mean just you personally. I mean the entire group.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody said anything about that. The people were unwashed, they were neglected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the prison authorities, on the 10th of December, did they -- said that you had to co-ordinate sending of a team with General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he was not responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you and the group that was there on that visit mention Colonel Papic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And on the 10th of December, 1991, this meeting in Sremska Mitrovica, was it attended by General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had the honour of ever personally meeting General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know his deputy, Colonel -- or, actually, do you know who his deputy was?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not meet either of them. Whoever that was, they would have probably introduced themselves to me as such, but nobody ever introduced themselves to me as General Vasiljevic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the name --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And was he there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the name of the person you mentioned in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked about the name Tumanov. I am repeating it.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of that last name. I know that there was a general, maybe he was a colonel, but I believe that he was a general. I never met him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask that the prisoners be handed over to you? Did you ask that the prisoners from Sremska Mitrovica be handed over to you, the government of the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never at any place asked for the prisoners of war to be handed over to me because I was not responsible for taking care of prisoners of war. Exclusively, in accordance with the law, that was something that was the responsibility of the Yugoslav People's Army. I knew what my duties and responsibilities were, and I also knew what their duties and rights and responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to repeat. Yes, I understand that you personally didn't ask for that. Did anybody from the group ask for that, Hadzic, Bogunovic, or anyone else who was with you there at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had they asked for that, I would have had the right and I would have used that right to warn them that these were the rights that were not ours, that we could not exercise these rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, were there any threats with weapons? Did any one of you threaten to use weapons if these demands of yours were not fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody made any threats with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you accuse General Vasiljevic of releasing prisoners without consulting you, meaning you personally and the government of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know why the prisoners were being released. I didn't know whose fault that was, if it was anybody's fault. And then I didn't know that General Vasiljevic was behind that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did any of you invite General Vasiljevic to lunch?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had he been there, perhaps we would have invited him. I believe that I would not have gone to that lunch, but as he wasn't there, we couldn't have invited him in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document is signed by Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic. Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us whether, after this meeting on the 10th of December, if you went to lunch to any of these officers [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not go to lunch to -- with any of these officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. The time for the second break; 30 minutes as well. We will be back at 12.45. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we see, please, tab 583. It is document 3028 from the Prosecution Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susa, do you know the person who is at the right side of the photograph, this adult shown?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, from what I can see, and this is Colonel Bogdan Vujic. Yes, it is him, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you notice him perhaps at the meeting in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not at the meeting in Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him perhaps in the Velepromet yard?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Bogdan Vujic, without his cap, in the Sremska Mitrovica KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic introduced himself as the commander of the city at the meeting in Velepromet, and he told you about the imposition of the military rule. Are you able to tell us what the situation was, if you know, regarding the authority of the army in areas where combat had finished in areas captured by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact whether the combat was over or not, the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY applied about the conduct of the army during imminent danger of war. In all those territories, the army had the absolute right to act on military and civilian matters. This was not in dispute. All we were required to do was to offer them co-operation in -- in the civilian sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us until when the military rule was in force in SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this was sometime until May or June 1992. Or, more specifically, after the new Yugoslavia was formed and after the adoption of the constitution in Zabljak, when Serbia and Montenegro decided to create the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the military authorities were trying to establish some co-operation with civilian authorities, or did they try to establish civilian authorities, or did they have any arrangements with the government of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They paid lip service to this, but they didn't actually do anything. They only addressed us when the problems grew to such an extent that they couldn't control them anymore. In every military structure, there was a contact person, a point man, for dealing with civilian issues, but even that officer didn't find it necessary to consult us in many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document from the screen into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3028 receives number D220, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, D19. It is tab 634.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order. It's not legible. Rather, the date is not legible. However, we believe that it was sent on the 20th of November. I wanted to ask you about a few things in this document, inviting your comments. You will see that under bullet point 2, the longest part says that work -- that the command has to work to establish civilian authorities in municipalities. According to the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian District of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem, the municipalities are Beli Manastir, Vukovar, Dalj, Vinkovci, with its seat in Mirkovci and Osijek with its seat in Tenja. On the 20th of November, was there a decision, as it says here, issued by the Assembly of the Serbian District of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, and Western Srem determining and defining the municipalities as listed here?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Great National Assembly made that decision subsequently, not in the form of decision because these issues are not resolved by issuing any decisions. This should be the Law on Territorial Organisation. I worked on that. It's not a decision, and in any case, that was passed after the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although you have already referred to this law, let me ask you once again. Before the passing of that law, was there a decision of that kind? Did this decision pre-exist the law?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's no decision that could be made on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 4 in this decision. It says here: "The established organs of authority are defined as the organs of authority that were established after the place was liberated under the leadership of organs of authority of the SO of Baranja, Eastern Slavonija, and Western Srem." Is it true that this sentence was applied as of the 20th November onwards?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only after the Law on Territorial Organisation came into effect. It defined the municipalities and its seats very precisely. We were the ones who appointed presence of Executive Councils, and then in their turn, they proposed their associates in consultations with the locals. When it comes to the Town Command and whether they're going to meddle with this, I believe that this decision is very self-explanatory. They very often meddled in political issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the local bodies of authority besides appointing presence of Executive Councils, did the local bodies of authority become appointed by the government or somebody else? Who appointed them?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were nominated by the government. Or, rather, in the hierarchy, there's the government, the municipalities, the local communes, and it would be the councils of the municipalities that appointed bodies at the lowest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be following the rules and regulations, but I'm not asking you about rules and regulations. I was probably not very precise in my question. What I wanted to ask you was whether you know how things were done in practice. Who was it who appointed those people in local communes and in the local bodies of authority? I'm talking about the practical part, not what it said in the decision about the Executive Councils.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer can't be simple because things were not approached everywhere in the same way. Let's start with Ilok. There was a drastic situation there. Military administration was introduced and the Town Command decided who directors would be, who members of the local communes would be. It also defined the composition of the police bodies, everything. Ilok comprises several villages such as Opatovac, Mohovo, and Sarengrad, and things were done in the same way on -- in these villages. In some other places like, for example, Mirkovci, where the local authorities [Realtime transcript read in error "military"] had been more powerful from before, they resisted those change-overs that the army sometimes insisted on and the situation was pretty much status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this decision, it says that the seat of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is in Dalj. Was the seat of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in Dalj on 28 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seat was never in Dalj. It was always in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here at the very bottom in the last sentence of this decision that Srbobran Bibic is the government commissioner for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In answer before the last one, it's recorded in the transcript: In some other places like, for example, Mirkovci where the military had been more powerful from before, they resisted ..." I believe the witness said "where the local authorities" or the civilian authorities. I don't think he said that the military had been more powerful than before they resisted changes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter confirms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that's on the record now. Thank you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was about Srbobran Bibic whose mentioned in the last sentence. Was Srbobran Bibic the government commissioner for Vukovar? Did the government appoint Srbobran Bibic as its commissioner for Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srbobran Bibic, also known as Rajko Bibic, ten or 15 days after the date indicated in here - and this confuses me somewhat - was appointed as the president of the Executive Council of Vukovar municipality by the government, not as its commissioner, as far as I know, and I'm almost sure that I am correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, could you please tell us something about the Vance Plan. What was the position of the government and the population in general in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem towards this proposal?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposal of the Vance Plan did not meet the support of the people in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem because of the way it envisaged the deployment of peacekeeping forces. People demanded from us to try and to affirm the idea that, according to the Vance Plan, somewhat altered, the peacekeeping forces of the United Nations should be deployed between the two warring parties. That proposal did not take off the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in some debates and discussions surrounding the adoption of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I participated in the work of a large gathering which was chaired by the people from the Presidency of the SFRY. I was there on day one. I believe that its work extended to the next day, when I was not present. However, I took the floor on the first day and my contribution was to oppose the deployment of UN peacekeepers in the depth of our territory. Unfortunately, I was right. My discussion was very -- in that sense, very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that the witness said the last sentence in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please ask the witness to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it was recorded that you said, as your last sentence --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My last sentence was: Unfortunately, I was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, you were recorded as saying: [In English] "My discussion was very -- in that sense, very good."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My discussion at the session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your answer did you say -- listen carefully, I'm going to repeat in English. I'm going to read this back to you. You said, allegedly: [In English] "My discussion was very -- in that sense, very good." [Interpretation] Did you indeed say that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that. My discussion at the Presidency session was very correct in view of the fact of what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So this was a misunderstanding. Why did you want the peacekeepers to be deployed on the separation line? Why did everybody want that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was the only and safe guarantee that there would be no more conflicts between the warring parties. They would act as a buffer zone, and the United Nations troops would be able to exert authority on the separation line and act as a buffer zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since that was your position, what was the position of Yugoslav authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their position was different from mine. They said that there could be no longer any delays in establishing peace in the war-affected areas. Nearly all representatives of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia spoke words to that effect. And as the debate went on and as our people heard their reasons, they moved to the side of the Presidency members and the idea that the Vance Plan should be adopted and applied at all cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told what could happen if the Croatian forces violated the cease-fire and entered the protected area?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were serious guarantees from the people from the Presidency that we -- that any sort -- any kind of assistance would be forthcoming and that we would be guaranteed protection, if any such thing would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you also discuss the regulations that would be implemented in the area where UN peacekeepers would be deployed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that my question at that Presidency session was to that effect. We were told that there would be a transition period and that the regulations in effect at that time would continue to be in effect during that transition period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have just mentioned Ilok in one of your answers. I would like to ask you whether the government had any contacts with Ilok after October 1991, when a large number of Croats moved out from that town and from that general area.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For several months after the departure of a large number of Croats, and they were mostly people who were able-bodied and could be considered military conscripts, we didn't have any contacts with the military administration in Ilok. That contact was established after the arrival of a large number of displaced persons from Western Slavonia to a place across the Danube from Ilok, and that is Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports or information, either from military authorities or any other official information, as to what was going on in Ilok during the relevant period of time, i.e., from the moment the Croatian population moved out until some months later?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had inofficial [as interpreted] information which proved to be very correct at the end of the day. The military is in charge of every -- everything in that area. They were involved in military issues as well as in all segments of civilian life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you officially request from the military authorities in Ilok to provide you with some information about the situation over there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The government put me and Mr. Vojnovic in charge, as well as Mr. Boro Bogunovic, of establishing contact with the military authorities in Ilok. I went to talk to the town commander, Colonel Belic. I explained to him why I was there, and I told him that we wanted to establish full co-operation because we had common problems. One of them was a large number of refugees who wanted to move into the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Mr. Belic did not show any understanding for the reasons mentioned by myself, and I returned to Erdut. I told Mr. Goran Hadzic about the reception I had met and then he wrote an official letter to Mr. Belic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up D30, tab 635.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this letter and tell us if that is the letter you mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a part of this letter. There is a continuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move to the next page. I believe there's one more page in English. I think it ends on page 4. [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is stated in this letter that the government does not know under what circumstances the military rule was imposed. What did they mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The circumstances under which this military rule is operating in Ilok for so long are unclear. The town commander was unable to prove with a single document his position in town. It was unclear who appointed him to that position in the first place. We didn't even know if he was a counterpart from the other side whom we should address in dealing with these problems, and my first conversation with him was, in fact, an attempt to get some kind of information, to inquire. But in this conversation, he was very arrogant and refused any further contact and rejected the possibility that we would be involved in establishing civilian authorities and restoring normal conditions in SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this letter, you asked, among other things, to be able to have an insight into the accounts of businesses and enterprises. Tell me, why did you make this request and was it met?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilok remained completely intact as a town. There was absolutely no damage or war devastation. There were several economic entities in Ilok that had a very successful business. They never ceased operating. For instance, it was the brick-works Razvitak, the winery Ilok, Agrokomerc, a textile industry called Iteks, and we wanted to inventory their assets. It was the territory of SBWS, and it was the property of the people who lived there. But regrettably we had information that turned out to be correct, to the effect that large amounts of property were being taken to Serbia unlawfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you given access to their assets and accounts?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this stage, no. Only much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This letter also mentions that JNA was the exclusive overseer of resettlement in Ilok; is that correct? Did the government have any part in it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as part of the Croatian population left Ilok, the JNA came in; specifically the units of the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina. They took possession of several facilities and started to dispose of the remaining buildings under criteria that were never clearly established, but mostly they were bringing just their own friends and family, accommodating them in the town, giving them jobs. They simply had absolute control over the area and did as they pleased. They made their own decisions, appointing general managers. They brought people from Serbia, they made arrangements with them on the further development of the town and further activities. And throughout that time in Ilok and the surrounding places, Opatovac, Mohovo, Sarengrad, and Sotin, they just moved people in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The letter mentions that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was going to rise earlier. I just want to check the document. Mr. Zivanovic represented that in this letter the military says that they were the exclusive overseer of resettlement in Ilok. I don't see that in the letter. I was wondering if he could just point it to me. Perhaps I'm missing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is in -- at previous page of English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, it's on page 2. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read out from the translation on the screen. This text is underlined: [In English] "The government has been told that the settling of Ilok went on rather well and that your command was competent in all matters. Naturally we are not bothered by this," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution would ask, Your Honours, that in the future, that Defence counsel use the language in the letter. I think that is open to interpretation what that sentence which was just read means and it's important to put the language to the witness so -- so as not to mislead or lead the witness in a certain direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zivanovic, I still didn't find it on -- on the page on the screen. Could you help -- assist me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is underlined. Paragraph, in English, at the screen. It is -- it begins with: "The government has been told that the settling of Ilok went on rather well ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see -- see it now. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was also said here that you were not informed of the criteria for resettlement. When I say "you," I mean the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. We were not informed of the criteria, and the whole truth is that these criteria did not even exist. We were just trying to be polite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, was the government asked to take any part in this process of resettlement? At any stage, did the government -- was the government asked by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, everything was done to stop the government from any participation in the resettlement process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is also said in this letter that you do not want to pre-empt any military or political solutions. What was this a reference to?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you understand, in this situation which involved a large inflow of refugees into Backa Palanka, the Croatian Operation Flash had already happened, and a large number of refugees were heading for Vojvodina in Serbia and other areas, including Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. While receiving these people, we were not thinking that these people would not have the possibility of returning to their homes in Baranja, Slavonia and other places in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You used the term "Operation Flash." Are you sure that operation happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people who came from Western Slavonia, they came as a result of military pressure by Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of status were they supposed to receive when they arrived in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or, specifically, Ilok? What was the government's idea about their stay there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were temporarily resettled places, accommodated in housing that they had the right to occupy only temporarily. That status is very important, and it was a reflection of our desire to help those people in those times, in that situation, in the only way we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was the government looking for some place to accommodate its own members? Did it ask for such accommodation from military authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And I'm coming back to the old story and the eviction of our property from the winery. This was the first opportunity for two or three ministries to get some offices, and we thought it would be a good idea if they were in Ilok. From back then until this point, we still operated without any offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you one letter that was sent out to the Town Command of Ilok on the same day as this letter. It's a regular report that the command of Ilok sent on the same day to its superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P1708. Tab 657.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the tenth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Occupation of empty houses continues in the territory of the command of the town of Ilok's area of responsibility. Occupation is taking place without the knowledge or approval of the command of the town of Ilok. The Presidency of SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem has not thus far given an announcement regarding the way and the conditions of settlement, which places this command into a very complex situation. At the same time, ethnic Croatian inhabitants are under pressure to leave this territory." Do you know whether there was any resettlement in that area that was not approved by the Town Command of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typical conflation frequently used at that time by the army. How was it possible that the area of responsibility of these units of Ilok somebody could enter an area, temporarily resettle there without them knowing? It's simply incredible. It runs counter to all their abilities and competences on the ground. It is was not us who set the criteria for resettlement. It was them. They did only things that suited them. Any involvement on our part would only be a bother for them. I perfectly understand their reasoning. I don't understand -- approve it but I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of an announcement they are referring to in paragraph 10? What kind of announcement was expected of you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the basis for this report was the letter we just looked at a moment ago. What the commander is doing here is actually self-defence. He's putting up his guard against any problem that we might create in the future for them and any issues that we were intending to raise, and it was clear that we were going to blame the Town Command of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P371. Tab 658. No, I think I made a mistake. We've seen this before. Yes, it's tab 574, and the exhibit is P378.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This report of 9 December, which means before your letter and before the other letter we saw a moment ago, was sent by the Town Command of Ilok to their superior command. They report about the situation in the area and the organisation of civilian life. They say that in Ilok and the villages enumerated here, including Lovas, no civilian authorities have been established and there is only one person dealing with all business in local offices. To the best of your knowledge, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's completely correct. It's just that the reasons for this are explained differently by us and the army. We think this was happening because we were not allowed to get into that area, whereas they pretend that we don't exist and, in fact, they were not giving us any access.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 2, it says that in the territory of the Town Command, TO Staffs have not been established and do not exist. To the best of your knowledge, is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 3, it says that a police station has been established in Ilok and one of its squads has been detached and posted to the village Lovas and that it was formed by the MUP of Serbia and is now under the authority of the SAO Baranja, Slavonia, Western Srem. In carrying out its tasks, the police station is subordinated to the command of the town of Ilok. Can you please tell us whether what is stated here is correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely as it is written it is correct and it proves the imbalance of all of their writing. It is not correct that it was under our jurisdiction, the police station, and then again they note that it's subordinated to the Town Command. So how is it possible that we established it but we are subordinated to them? We did not establish it. Of course not. They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just one second because there are a number of assertions here. Let's look at the text. It says here that the police station was formed by the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But that it is under the authority of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. What I'm interested in is whether it's correct that it was formed under the Serbian MUP but it was under your authority?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was formed by the Serbian MUP. It's not correct that it's under the authority of the SBWS. And in carrying out its tasks, the police station is subordinated to the command of the town of Ilok, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, since you said that what is said -- stated here is not correct, was the SBWS government consulted at all regarding the police that is referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SBWS government was not consulted in any single activity or specific action by the military authorities in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at D45, please. This is tab 654.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a request by the Town Command of Ilok, seeking an explanation about a request of the refugees to settle in Ilok and settlements within the area of responsibility of the town of Ilok. It is stated here that there was a large number of abandoned houses and apartments.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to comment what I'm looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. And that the Town Command is receiving requests from refugees to settle the abandoned -- to settle in the abandoned houses. Instructions are being sought. Could you please tell us if this accurately reflects the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you put all the information of theirs next to each other and read it, then you can see how they are actually conveying half-truths, but then, after all, you can come to a conclusion -- and this is how they know, after all, that they know who was moving into the abandoned properties. They were receiving a large number of requests. Now that the number of requests is too large and they cannot control it anymore, so now they're asking for help. Before, when they were determining the dynamics, they were able to work on their own and deal with it without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these instructions are dated the 28th of November, 1991. What I'm interested in is whether, in that period, did you, as the government, receive any requests for people to settle in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no. Then, we did not receive any single request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time, did they address you for some kind of consultations or agreements or anything regarding this problem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never addressed us unless they were in a difficult situation or we were very persistent and, thus, forced them to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you were informed or if you had information whether they effectively controlled the territories they were in possession of?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were many soldiers there, a lot of equipment. They had the legal authority to act, but not act badly but act correctly and properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit 6038, tab 658 from the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a regular daily report of the 30th of November, 1991, again from the Ilok Town Command. Could you please look at paragraph 2, where the places that are affected in this territory are referred to. In item 6, the tasks and assignments are referred to from the Ilok Town Commander with the focus on the control of movements, the immediate security of the said places, and the carrying out of tasks relating to the command post. According to what you know, was this correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was correct. Otherwise, the chief, the lieutenant-colonel, would be subject to disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, after you came to Ilok on the 23rd of December and later, was the situation the same. In other words, were the Ilok Town Command units still controlling the movement in their area and directly providing security for the places that are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what they were doing. They were doing their part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6038 receives number D221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you mentioned, among other things, that the Ilok Town Command appointed directors of certain companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D2196. It is tab 466.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the decisions that we found. Are you able to tell us if you knew that this company, Agrokomerc, had the following director appointed by the Ilok Town Command?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a good friend of mine. He was a good friend then and is still my good friend. In this way, he was appointed a director. It wasn't only him. All the directors of economic companies, kindergartens, the cultural institutions, all of those posts were filled by the commander of the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2196 receives number D222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D2493. It is tab 490.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another decision on a director's appointment. This time it's the Razvitak company. Did you know that this person was appointed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Milovan Buha very well, and I met him in Ilok when he was already the director of this company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that the document bears the date 30th of January, 1992. Are you able to tell us approximately how long did the Ilok Town Command decide on the appointment of directors of commercial enterprises?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that this is linked to certain laws, to the way things functioned, and also it has to do with Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because he had a hand in regulating relationships in this way in the town of Ilok. But already, by the spring of that year, by March, all of this gained a slightly different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1683. It is tab 645. Sorry, I would tender this document from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Zivanovic, that this document is already in evidence as 14 -- D141, if I'm not wrong. Admitted on the 15th of July, 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is my error in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1683. It is tab 645.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another regular daily report from November 1991. It refers to various activities in the Ilok Town Command area of responsibility. I would like to ask you to look at paragraph 7. It's on the second page of the original. And, among other things, this paragraph talks about intensive normative work that is being done on establishing local commands and ensuring their functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the next page in the English translation, please, where it says that in the course of paramilitary units, Dusan Silni Detachment were chased out and parts of the local TO were placed under a single command of TO commands present in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is this: Did the Ilok Town Command have enough forces, effect force, in your estimation, to regulate the conduct, the movement, and generally the presence of paramilitary formations in its territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did. There was a large number of well-armed soldiers that were under their command. They were at -- they had quite a significant amount of equipment at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you one more exhibit for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is P1709, tab 659.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a letter that you wrote to the Ilok Town Command, if you recall. And in the letter, you talk about the temporary moving in in the territory of Ilok and a meeting is being scheduled. Do you remember this letter?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now to look at the attachments to this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the following pages of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a list here of the inhabitants, and you can also see in the following pages that there are also maps attached besides the handwritten lists. I think that you looked at these documents.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, are -- were all the other pages attached to your letter? In other words, were you the one who attached these documents to your letter or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attach the documents. These documents were drafted by the army. My letter does not contain the rest of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, did you attach any other documents, any lists with your letter?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Otherwise, I would have stated so and I would have listed the attachments to the letter. And I think you can also see that there are military stamps on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- we should call it a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Susa, we expect you to be back tomorrow at 9.00. You remain a witness and under oath, and I explained yesterday to you what that means in terms of discussing your testimony with other people or having contact with the parties. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. And I am sticking to that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
